title: A Decision Log Busy Teams Will Actually Keep
summary: A decision log is a few lines per decision: what you chose, what you dropped, why, who owns it and when to revisit. A format busy teams actually keep up with.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
The call ends with everyone nodding. It feels like agreement until Tuesday. One person remembers the team picked the simpler rollout. Another remembers the risky customer segment was left out. A third thinks the whole thing is still open. Nobody was careless. The decision just evaporated when the call ended.

Busy teams decide things in fragments: a Slack thread, a quick call after standup, a comment on a PR, one sentence from a stakeholder. Each piece makes sense at the time. A week later nobody can put them back together, and when memory is the only record, the most recent or the loudest version wins.

A decision log fixes this cheaply. It's a short written record per decision, kept where the next person will look. Below: what goes in an entry, where it lives, which decisions deserve one and how to change your mind later without a fight.

What goes in an entry

Architecture teams have done this for years under the name ADR, short for architecture decision record. Michael Nygard's 2011 post Documenting Architecture Decisions set the shape most teams still use: a title, the context (the forces at play), the decision written as "We will...", a status, and the consequences, good and bad. He kept each record to "one or two pages" for a blunt reason: "Large documents are never kept up to date."

For everyday product and delivery decisions you can go lighter. Seven fields cover nearly everything:

## 2026-11-03 · Bulk discount: staged rollout
Question:  How do we launch the new bulk discount?
Decision:  Ship behind a flag to 10% of shops, then 50%, then everyone.
Dropped:   Big-bang launch. Fast, but no way back if pricing is wrong.
           Wait for the full reporting dashboard. Two more weeks.
Why:       A pricing bug hits revenue directly. A flag turns it off in minutes.
Owner:     An (backend). Mai (product) signs off each step.
Revisit:   If refund requests climb above normal during the 10% stage.

The "Dropped" line is the one people skip, and it's the most useful. Martin Fowler's advice on decision records is to "explicitly list all the serious alternatives that were considered, together with their pros and cons" (Architecture Decision Record). Six months later, the first thing a new teammate asks is usually "why didn't we just do X?" If X is on the list with a reason, that conversation takes thirty seconds.

The "Revisit" line does a different job. It names the evidence that would reopen the decision, so changing course later becomes a planned step and nobody has to admit defeat.

Why it's worth the five minutes

The main payoff is being able to find the reason later. Nygard describes the newcomer who runs into a strange past decision with no reason attached. They're left with two bad options: "Blindly accept the decision" or "Blindly change it." One line of "why" removes both.

Spotify's engineering team saw the same thing after rolling out ADRs widely. Future team members "are able to read a history of decisions," new owners of a system "can quickly get up to speed," and teams found it easier to agree on shared practices (When Should I Write an Architecture Decision Record).

Writing it also helps in the moment. Fowler notes that "the act of writing them helps to clarify thinking, particularly with groups of people." Typing "We will..." where everyone can see it is often when two people discover they agreed to different things. Much better to learn that on Monday than in production.

And it takes the heat out of disagreements. Without a record, people argue from memory, and memory feels personal. With one, the team can say: "Here's what we knew then. Here's what changed. Let's decide again." Nobody has to defend the old choice like it's their reputation.

Keep it where the work is

If writing a decision down takes longer than making it, the habit dies within a month. So keep entries short and keep them close to the work:

  • Code and architecture decisions go in the repo, next to the code. Nygard used doc/arch/adr-NNN.md, and Fowler calls keeping records in the source repository "the common advice."
  • Product and rollout decisions go in the epic or ticket, or in one running log page the whole team bookmarks.
  • Decisions made in a meeting go in the meeting notes, linked from the log. Keeping meeting notes close to decisions covers that side.

Pick one home per kind of decision and tell the team where it is. A log scattered across five tools is just another pile of fragments.

Which decisions deserve an entry

Not all of them. A button label or a variable name doesn't need one. Spotify's rule is to write a record "whenever a decision of significant impact is made," and to let each team decide what "significant" means. A practical test is future confusion. Write it down if any of these is true:

  • Someone will probably ask "why?" within the next six months.
  • It's hard to undo. Jeff Bezos calls these one-way doors in his 2015 shareholder letter, and they're the ones worth slowing down for.
  • The trade-off lands on another team.
  • New evidence could reasonably flip it.
  • You just picked the standard way to do something, and you'd like the next person to reuse it instead of inventing a second one.

Changing your mind without rewriting history

Decisions change, and that's healthy. What you shouldn't do is edit the old entry in place so it looks like you always thought this. Nygard and Fowler both recommend keeping the old record and marking it superseded, with a link to the new one. Fowler is firm about it: "Once an ADR is accepted, it should never be reopened or changed - instead it should be superseded."

That chain is worth more than it looks. Read a few superseded entries in a row and you can see how the team's thinking moved: which risks kept coming back, which assumptions broke, where you picked the simple option on purpose. It's the closest thing a team has to a memory that doesn't depend on who's still around.

Try this week

  • Pick the last decision your team argued about twice and write it up with the seven fields above.
  • Agree on one home for the log and pin the link in your team channel.
  • At the end of your next decision meeting, have someone type the "Decision" and "Dropped" lines before everyone leaves.
  • The next time you reverse a decision, write a new entry and mark the old one superseded.

Decision logs work best once the work itself is clear. For the step before that, when a task is still fuzzy and everyone has a different picture of it, see Turning unclear work into shared notes.

faqs.a: A decision log is a short written record of each important team decision, kept where the next person will look. A useful entry has seven lines: the question, the decision, the options you dropped, why, who owns it, the date, and what evidence would make you revisit it. It's a lighter cousin of the architecture decision record (ADR) that Michael Nygard described in 2011.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a decision log and an ADR?
faqs.a: An ADR (architecture decision record) is one kind of decision log, focused on architecture. Nygard's format has a title, context, decision, status and consequences, kept to one or two pages and stored in the code repository. A team decision log uses the same idea for product, rollout and process decisions, usually in fewer lines and wherever the team already works.

faqs.q: Which decisions should we write down?
faqs.a: Use future confusion as the test. Write it down if someone will probably ask why within six months, if it's hard to undo, if the trade-off affects another team, if new evidence could flip it, or if you just set a standard way of doing something. Small choices like button labels or variable names don't need an entry.

faqs.q: What should we do when a decision changes?
faqs.a: Write a new entry and mark the old one as superseded, with a link to the new decision. Don't edit the old entry in place. Both Michael Nygard and Martin Fowler recommend this, and Fowler says an accepted record should never be reopened or changed. The chain of old and new entries shows how the team's thinking moved and why.

faqs.q: Where should a decision log live?
faqs.a: Close to the work. Architecture and code decisions belong in the repository next to the code, which is the common advice for ADRs. Product and rollout decisions fit in the epic, the ticket or one running log page the team bookmarks. Pick one home per kind of decision and tell everyone, so the log doesn't become another scattered set of fragments.
